pronunciation.approximation: YAH-nus, long ā on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Latin Iānus begins with a consonantal i ([j]); the ā is long and the final -us short. Varro connected the name to ire, "to go," and Cicero to ianua, "door" — both folk etymologies of a genuinely old Italic god. The restoration Iānus keeps the long ā, the form dictionaries print; the temple calendars abbreviate him simply KAL, the Kalends he owns.

domains.title: The God of the Door
domains.subtitle: Beginnings, Gates, and the Two Faces
domains.lead: Iānus has no Greek equivalent and no mythology of adventure: he is Rome's god of passages themselves — doors, bridges, beginnings, the month that opens the year. His two faces look both ways because every threshold faces two worlds.

cards.name: The Gates of War
cards.desc: The Ianus Geminus, open while Rome fought, closed in peace — shut only a handful of times in seven centuries.

cards.name: Bifrons
cards.desc: The two-faced one: past and future, entrance and exit, watched simultaneously.

cards.name: January
cards.desc: Iānuārius — his month still opens the civil year of half the world.

cards.name: The As
cards.desc: His double face stamped the earliest Roman bronze coinage, with the prow of a ship on the reverse.

mythology.lead: Ovid's Fasti gives him the one great scene: the poet asks the two-faced god why he looks both ways, and Iānus answers for himself — the only extended self-explanation any Roman god gets in verse. Around it stand the war gates, the threshold nymph, and the oldest Roman 'history' of all: Saturn's flight to his kingdom.

myths.title: Fasti 1: The God Explains Himself
myths.text: Ovid opens his calendar with the boldest interview in Roman poetry: he asks Iānus why, alone among the gods, he sees both behind and before (Fasti 1.63–288). The god answers at length. Whatever you see — sky, sea, earth — all things are closed and opened by my hand; I preside over the gates of heaven with the gentle Seasons; I was called Chaos once, for I am the ancient confusion out of which order came. Then he teaches the poet why the year begins in winter: December's fires end, the sun turns, and the new year opens with the returning light — a beginning honored at the threshold, at the first word spoken across a door. No other Roman god narrates himself in verse; the door, characteristically, speaks for itself. The myth's quiet claim is that beginnings are not a moment in time but a power over time — the hinge on which the year itself swings.

myths.title: Ianus Geminus: The Open Door of Empire
myths.text: Numa, the peace-king who followed Romulus, founded the rite that made the god a barometer of war: the double gates of the Ianus Geminus in the Forum stood open while Rome was at war and closed only in peace (Livy 1.19). Livy records that in the four centuries after Numa they had been shut exactly twice before Augustus — once in 235 BCE in the consulship of Titus Manlius — and Augustus boasted in his Res Gestae (13) of closing them three times. Later sources credited Nero with a closure after the Armenian settlement, and emperors of the third century repeated the gesture; Procopius saw the gates still standing in the sixth century. The arithmetic is the myth: an open temple as the default, peace so rare it needed a ceremony to announce. The god of beginnings watched a state for whom war was the standing condition — and held the door open accordingly.

myths.title: Carna and the Hawthorn
myths.text: Ovid's second January of folklore concerns the goddess of the hinge (Fasti 6.101–168). Carna had spent her youth outwitting her suitors — promising to meet each in a dark grove, then never coming — until she tried the trick on Iānus. The two-faced god, who cannot be crept up on, simply looked backward and saw her behind him; caught, she yielded, and the marriage made her mistress of the door's moving parts. Carna became the guardian of hinges and the health of children, honored on the Kalends of June with emmer porridge and lard set out at midnight to keep the night-hags from the cradles. It is Rome's most domestic theology: a marriage between the god of the threshold and the goddess of the hinge, celebrated in bean-and-bacon at the kitchen door. The myth makes the household's smallest mechanism — the swinging door — a point of contact with the highest cosmic one, and both of them need a woman to keep them true.

myths.title: Saturn's Flight to Janus' Kingdom
myths.text: The oldest Roman 'history' makes Janus a king before he was a door. When Jupiter drove his father Saturn from Olympus, the exile fled west and was received in Italy by Janus, who then ruled over Latium — so Ovid tells it (Fasti 1.233–254), and Virgil before him (Aeneid 8.319–325). Janus shared his kingdom with the refugee, and under their joint rule the people lived in the Saturnia regna: no walls, no laws, no war, the earth giving fruit without labor. Saturn taught the planting of vines and grain; when he departed, the memory remained in his hill, his feast, and his month of plenty, while Macrobius (Saturnalia 1.7–8) collects the rites that kept the partnership warm each December. The myth makes Janus the host of history itself: every arrival from elsewhere — god, refugee, year — enters the world through his doorway, and he receives them all with the same two faces, one grieving the home lost, one greeting the home found.

lore.syncretism: The Etruscans knew a two-faced gate-spirit (Culsans, paired with the one-faced Culsu), and Iānus absorbed that numinous door-power early. Having no Greek twin, he puzzled the mythographers: some aligned him with the sky, some with Chaos itself — Ovid reports both. Medieval Europe kept him as the face of January in calendar art, and the Renaissance restored him on coins and doorways. Modern science borrowed him wholesale: "Janus particles" (two-faced colloids), the Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes that open two signaling paths at once, and "Janus-faced" as the standard diagnosis of ambivalence — the god of two ways of seeing became the name for the condition itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: January keeps his name on every calendar; the janitor keeps his keys in every school; 'Janus-faced' remains the standard charge in diplomacy and the standard diagnosis in literature. The Roman habit of naming him first — at marriages, departures, consulates, and the first word of every prayer — survives in the New Year's toast, the doorstep superstition, and the instinct to look back before stepping forward. Historians read the rarity of his closed gates as Rome's autobiography: a republic that could count its years of peace on one hand, and a god whose open temple was the weather of empire. Every doorway ritual ever performed is, knowingly or not, his small surviving liturgy.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Iānus is the god of the door you are standing in. Every beginning contains its end; every entrance is also an exit watched from the other side. He does not judge the passage — he is the passage. To honour him is to pause at thresholds: to look back once, look forward once, and only then walk through.

Modernity made him its secret patron: every pivot, every launch, every new year, every door held open for a stranger is his small liturgy. The Romans began everything — journeys, marriages, consulates, the year itself — by naming him first, on the principle that a beginning honoured is half accomplished. His two faces are the correct posture for any threshold: gratitude backward, attention forward, and then — the god's whole point — through.

It is no accident that Rome's rarest public celebration was his closed gates: peace was so unusual it needed a god's doorway to mark it. The open gates were the default, the ordinary weather of a martial state — and the god watched both conditions with the same two faces, praising neither. His neutrality is the lesson: thresholds do not judge what passes through them; they only insist that passing is a choice, and that someone remember to look both ways first.

lore.archaeology: The Ianus Geminus stood in the Forum near the Curia; its bronze gates survived into late antiquity (Procopius describes them), though the structure's exact footprint is debated. His most durable monument is numismatic: the heavy cast bronze aes grave of the 3rd century BCE bears the double-faced head — one of the earliest portrait-types of Roman coinage — and the denarius tradition continued it. A small shrine of Ianus on the Janiculum, the hill that probably bears his name, tied the god to Rome's western gate.
